segments.text: In a workshop, participation doesn't happen  by accident. It happens by design. As much as
we'd like to think that free-flowing conversation  allows people to jump in and share their thoughts,
sometimes the most deliberately generous thing  you can do is provide structure in the workshop
so that discussions follow a format and have  boundaries and constraints around who speaks,
how they speak, and how often they speak. In  this video, I share with you three deliberately
generous structures that help people share the  air so that everyone gets a chance to be heard.
Hi, I'm Kerri Price. I'm the  founder of The Facilitators Network,
and I use the principles of deliberate  generosity to make sure that no meeting
or workshop is ever wasted. I've been a  professional facilitator for 20-odd years,
and in that time, I've led thousands of  meetings, workshops, and community conversations.
Nowadays, I help other trainers  and facilitators do it well, too.
In a perfect world, everyone in a  workshop would share the air. They'd
actively listen to one another. They'd  respect people's opinions and thoughts.
But we know we don't live in a perfect world.  So sometimes creating structure or boundaries
around a conversation is exactly what's needed  to make sure that everyone's voices are heard.
The thing is, not every structure  is right for every situation.
So it's important to have a bunch of  different tools and different structures
in your back pocket so you can use the right  structure in the right way with the right group
every time. In this video, I share  three of my favorite structures
that work in different contexts. You'll  want to stick around for all three.
Activity one is called Twice Around  the Block, and it uses one or two
of these big ropes that you might get from  a sailing shop or a hardware store. A nice,
big, thick rope that people can hold  onto. How it works is you grab the rope,
pull it out, and tie a knot in the two  ends so that you end up with a big loop.
You then invite people to stand in a circle, and  they're all holding on to a piece of the rope.
The person who is holding the rope closest to  the knot becomes the first person to speak.
As they start speaking, people start moving  the rope around the circle, hand over fist,
until the knot passes by the speaker two  times. Hence, Twice Around the Block.
I most often use Twice Around the  Block for light-hearted conversations,
maybe connection rounds where  people are introducing themselves,
or maybe reflections at the end of the  day. I wouldn't use it so much if it was a
robust discussion where decisions or  important things are needing to take place.
Now, what's interesting about this structure
is that people tend to move the rope in pace  with how they talk. So, if they're a fast talker,
they will start moving the rope quite  quickly. And if they're a slow talker,
they might move the rope more slowly. As a  facilitator, you need to be mindful of this
and make sure that others in the group aren't  trying to speed up or slow down the process.
What I love about this activity is it's a  little bit light-hearted and fun. It doesn't
feel really rule-bound or like it has strict  conditions. You're standing, you're chatting,
and you're moving at the same time. When the  knot passes by the speaker for the first time,
it's a little bit of a warning  that they're halfway through.
And then, when it passes by the second time,  they need to wrap up their sharing. Wherever
the knot stops next, which is usually the person  beside them or perhaps one or two people along,
they then get to share next. And  again, it's Twice Around the Block.
Structure number two is called Signal Your Input.  And I tend to use this structure if I'm going into
a complex conversation where I know there might  be lots of different viewpoints, perhaps some
history between people in the group, where the  group dynamic might be a bit shaky, or I think
that there might be disagreement or side tracks  or side quests that people want to take us down.
And how it works is by using these  colored cards. So what I do at the
beginning of the session is I explain to  people that part of my job as a facilitator
is to keep the conversation on time and on  track. But often, we can spiral down rabbit holes
if people are asking questions, making comments,  and adding opinions all at the same time.
So, I introduce these colored cards as a way  for people to signal what their input might be.
The yellow card signals, "I have a question or I  need clarification about what's just been said."
The green card says, "I can provide clarification  for that question. I can answer that question
for that person." The blue card says, "I have an  opinion or a comment that I'd like to add to this
discussion." So, this is viewpoints, information,  comments, and opinions. The red card says, "Huh,
I have an observation about what's going on  in this discussion that might be helpful."
Now, what I love about this process,  as complicated as it sounds,
is that it helps me know who to call on  next. So, it's not just a case of who
might have their hand up. It's about what makes  the most sense here in terms of who speaks next.
I will always go to questions first  because there's no point in people
adding more comments or opinions if there are  people in the room who need clarification.
What I love about this structure is that it  makes it really easy for people to signal
what their input is going to be, and I  can call on people in a logical order.
I also like it because the colored cards do a  lot of the heavy lifting, and it lets people
signal to me what they're wanting to share  without them even having to open their mouths.
Structure three is called the Silent Start. And  I use this structure an awful lot of the time
in lots of different ways. And the Silent  Start is exactly how it sounds. When I open
up a conversation for discussion or I send  people into small groups for a discussion,
before doing that, I give people three minutes  to silently start the conversation on their own.
And what I mean by that is that I give  them two or three minutes on their own
to think about what they might like  to contribute to the discussion
and jot that down on a piece of paper. That  means when the discussion officially starts,
they've already done some thinking,  and they've got some notes to talk to.
Now, why this is really important is that  we know about one-third of any given room
have people who are internal processors.  In other words, the people who like to
internally process their ideas before they speak  them aloud. If you don't include a Silent Start
or give people a chance to think about what they'd  like to say before you start the conversation,
then one-third of the people in the room are  going to find it really hard to contribute.
You need to create that space so  that when the conversation starts,
everyone's on equal footing  around how they engage.
Of course, structure is not the only solution  to engagement. There are lots of other reasons
why people may not be engaging or may be holding  back and being quiet in a room. In my next video,
Facilitation Tools and Techniques  for Engaging Quiet Participants,
I share with you five reasons why  people may be quiet in your workshop,
and I give you some simple techniques  for overcoming each one of those reasons.
The video should be playing somewhere up here,  so just click on the link and go check it out.
